newsitem.title: UK: European gas rivals battle for market share.
newsitem.headline: European gas rivals battle for market share.

text.p: Rival European gas suppliers are battling to secure market share in anticipation of fast-growing demand from power generators and domestic users across the continent, analysts said on Tuesday.

International suppliers have moved quickly to win a string of new contracts as rising gas output, consumer pressure for clean energy, new gas-fired power technology and European Union deregulation combine to make natural gas Europe's fuel of choice for the next century.
The current spate of deals is not just driven by suppliers.

"Buyers are looking to secure gas in the light of liberalisation," said Neil Thomas, gas analyst at consultancy Wood Mackenzie. "Access to gas is a key factor in the development of competition and buyers are keen to retain their markets."
Last week saw several major deals signed to supply gas to western European consumers well into the next century.

One of Europe's biggest buyers, German industrial giant Ruhrgas AG, settled new purchases from Britain, Norway and the Netherlands, including a landmark deal with British Petroleum Co plc to purchase 15 billion cubic metres (bcm) (529.7 billion cu ft) over 15 years from the North Sea.
From 1998 the gas will flow through a new pipeline, the Interconnector, linking Britain to Belgium and from there to the whole European gas grid.

Ruhrgas extended an existing contract with Dutch Gasunie to at least 2022, increasing its contractual purchases over the period to 90 bcm. Ruhrgas also prolonged its contracts to buy gas from Norway's Ekofisk field, operated by Phillips Petroleum Co, until 2028.
Norway's multi-company Gas Negotiating Committee (GFU) also announced its first deal to supply gas to Italy's SNAM SpA, for six bcm a year over 25 years.
Suppliers are keen to secure sales contracts because output is growing as fast, or faster than, demand.
Russian producer Gazprom last week signed a preliminary agreement with Finland's Neste to consider the feasibility of building a pipeline across Finfland to deliver Russian gas to central Europe.
Gazprom, which accounts for some 60 percent of Europe's total imports, is already constructing the $40 billion Yamal-pipeline to supply Germany via Belarus and Poland.

Gazprom's board also recently approved a $2.5 billion project to build the world's deepest underwater gas pipeline, taking gas under the Black Sea to Turkey. These links are in addition to Russia's main export line which connects Siberian fields to western Europe through Ukraine.
Algeria has not been slow to respond to the growth in European demand and increased exports from its northern rivals.

The Gazoduc Maghreb-Europe, a pipeline connecting the giant gas fields of Hassi R'mel in the south of the country with Spain and Portugal via Morocco and the strait of Gibraltar, opened in December with an initial flow of 10 bcm a year.

The combined impact of projects in the North Sea, Russia and Algeria is for an increase in European supplies of at least 90 bcm a year by the end of the century, up a quarter from 377 bcm in 1995, analysts estimate.
The new gas supplies will be used in two main areas, for power generation and domestic use as a cooking and heating fuel.
"Gas will be displacing a lot of existing fuel sources," said Graham Shuttleworth, associate director of London-based National Economic Research Associates.
Coal, nuclear power and oil will feel the impact of increased gas use in power generation.
"Gas will cause the same problems for coal and nuclear power as it did in the UK," he said, referring to the rise in gas for power generation in Britain.
The big suppliers are also moving to maximise profits as gas demand grows, said Dutch gas consultant Floor Touber.

"They will move into the end part of the market where the margins are made. Large players at the upstream are moving down the chain, and getting involved in pipelines, distribution, even in setting up power generation."
